1.modern-en: Oedipus comes out to meet the suppliants crowding his palace steps, declaring that he has already taken action on their behalf. He announces he has sent Creon to the Delphic oracle and vows to do whatever the god commands to cleanse Thebes of its plague.

3.modern-en: Oedipus issues a public proclamation cursing the murderer of Laius and demanding that anyone with knowledge come forward. When Teiresias arrives and refuses to speak, Oedipus goads him with furious accusations — and is shaken when the prophet finally declares that Oedipus himself is the killer he seeks.

5.modern-en: Oedipus confronts Creon directly, accusing him of conspiring with Teiresias to steal the throne. He dismisses Creon's calm defence and threatens him with death or exile, relenting only under pressure from Jocasta and the Chorus.

7.modern-en: Oedipus tells Jocasta his fears: a detail she mentions — Laius killed at a crossroads — strikes him with dread. He recounts how he fled Corinth after an oracle warned him he would kill his father and marry his mother, and how he slew a group of travelers at a crossroads. He clings to a thin hope that the herdsman's account of many attackers will clear him.

9.modern-en: The news that Polybus is dead initially fills Oedipus with relief — proof, he thinks, that oracles lie. But the Corinthian messenger reveals that Polybus was not his real father; he was found as an infant on Mount Cithaeron. Oedipus presses urgently for the identity of his true parents despite Jocasta's desperate pleas to stop.

10.modern-en: The terrible truth closes in on Oedipus as the Herdsman confirms he gave away the infant — a child of Laius. Oedipus cries out that he is revealed as accursed — the killer of his father and the son and husband of his mother — then rushes inside.

11.modern-en: Oedipus bursts into the palace and finds Jocasta hanged. He tears the brooches from her robe and drives them into his own eyes. Blinded and wailing, he emerges before the Chorus, acknowledges Apollo has brought his fate to pass, and begs Creon to cast him out of Thebes. He says farewell to his daughters, entrusting them to Creon's care.

5.modern-en: Jocasta steps out of the palace to stop the argument between Oedipus and Creon, rebuking both for letting private quarrels erupt in public while Thebes suffers. She persuades Oedipus to spare her brother.

7.modern-en: Jocasta tries to ease Oedipus's fears by dismissing prophecy: an oracle once said Laius would be killed by his own son, yet that child was exposed on a hillside and Laius was slain by strangers at a crossroads — so oracles are not to be trusted. Her reassurance backfires when the detail of the crossroads only deepens Oedipus's dread.

8.modern-en: Jocasta enters the stage carrying offerings to Apollo's shrines, seeking divine help because Oedipus is too shaken to act rationally. Her prayer is interrupted by the arrival of the Corinthian Messenger with news of Polybus's death, which she takes as further proof that oracles are worthless.

9.modern-en: The Messenger's revelation that Oedipus was a foundling suddenly makes Jocasta understand the full truth before Oedipus does. She begs him desperately to stop his inquiry, saying only 'God pity you!' — then rushes into the palace in silence, which is her last appearance speaking.

11.modern-en: Jocasta does not appear alive on stage. The Second Messenger reports that she rushed to the bridal chamber, called on the name of the long-dead Laius, and hanged herself with a running noose — overwhelmed by the knowledge of what she had unknowingly done.

epithet.en: Brother of Jocasta, advisor to the king

1.modern-en: Creon returns from Delphi and delivers Apollo's command: the land is polluted by the unavenged murder of Laius, and Thebes must find and punish his killer. He provides Oedipus the few known facts — that Laius was killed at a crossroads, apparently by a band of thieves, with one survivor escaping.

4.modern-en: Creon hears that Oedipus has accused him of treason and comes before the Chorus to deny it, insisting he has no desire for the trouble and danger of kingship when he already shares in power without the burden.

5.modern-en: Creon defends himself calmly against Oedipus's furious accusations, arguing logically that a man who already enjoys power without responsibility would be mad to plot for the throne. He is acquitted only because the Chorus and Jocasta intercede; he leaves warning Oedipus that quick judgment reveals a quick temper.

11.modern-en: Creon arrives as the only figure of authority left standing. He gently leads the blinded Oedipus inside, away from public sight. He listens to Oedipus's requests — exile, burial for Jocasta, care for his daughters — responding with measured compassion but firm authority, reminding Oedipus that the gods, not he, will decide the terms of his exile.

3.modern-en: Teiresias arrives led by a boy and at first refuses to speak, saying his knowledge will bring no comfort to anyone. Goaded by Oedipus's fury and accusations, he finally declares that Oedipus is the murderer he is hunting, then delivers a chilling prophecy: the man so proud of his sight will one day be blind, a beggar driven from the land — revealed as both brother and father to his own children, both son and husband to his own mother.

epithet.en: Spokesman for the suffering people of Thebes

1.modern-en: The Priest leads the suppliants gathered at Oedipus's palace and speaks on their behalf, describing the plague devastating Thebes — blighted crops, dying livestock, women dying in childbirth. He appeals to Oedipus as the man who once solved the Sphinx's riddle, imploring him to find a way to save the city once more.

8.modern-en: The Messenger from Corinth arrives at the palace with news that Polybus, king of Corinth, has died of old age and the Corinthians wish Oedipus to become their king. He meets Jocasta first, who takes this as proof that Oedipus's fears about the oracle were groundless.

9.modern-en: Trying to ease Oedipus's remaining fear — that he might still marry his mother Merope — the Messenger reveals that Oedipus is not the blood son of Polybus and Merope at all. He himself received Oedipus as an infant on Mount Cithaeron from one of Laius's herdsmen and gave him to the childless Corinthian king. This disclosure, meant as a kindness, sets in motion the final unraveling of the truth.
